# CIA Triad

Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — the three properties any security control is ultimately
defending. Lab 09 of [[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]] defines the working vocabulary at the
point where it is needed, which is when a protocol has to be chosen rather than described.

## The definitions the lab uses

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Confidentiality** | protection against unauthorised access, while providing authorised users unobstructed access. Data is not disclosed to anyone without a valid need to know |
| **Integrity** | the data has not been altered in an unauthorised way. A third party capturing and modifying it should be detectable |
| **Availability** | the system is reachable and usable when needed — the property injection and flooding attacks target when they cannot read anything |
| **Authentication** | confirming the declared identity of a participant, to a level of certainty |
| **Authorization** | access control — confirming that an authenticated entity may use the requested resource |

The lab's own list foregrounds **authentication and authorization as separate entries**, and that is
the distinction worth carrying: they are not the same control, they fail differently, and the broken-
access-control class in [[web-application-injection]] is precisely what happens when a system
authenticates correctly and then never authorises.

**Non-repudiation** is the fourth property usually attached to the triad, and it is the one only
asymmetric cryptography supplies — see [[digital-signatures]].

## Which primitive provides which property

This is the mapping the course is building toward, and getting it wrong is the standard beginner
error:

| Property | Provided by |
|---|---|
| Confidentiality | encryption — a cipher and a mode, see [[block-cipher-modes]] |
| Integrity | a hash inside a MAC or a signature. **Encryption does not provide it** |
| Authentication (of an entity) | signatures plus a trust binding, see [[public-key-infrastructure]] |
| Authentication (of a message) | MAC / HMAC |
| Availability | rate limiting, redundancy, filtering — largely *not* a cryptographic problem |

The error the mapping prevents: an encrypted channel with no integrity protection can be tampered
with. Under a stream-like mode, flipping a ciphertext bit flips the corresponding plaintext bit, and
the recipient decrypts modified data with no indication anything happened. Confidentiality and
integrity are orthogonal, and every modern protocol provides both explicitly.

## What the lab measured

OpenVPN is analysed as the practical case: SSL/TLS for the handshake, HMAC with a digest for packet
integrity, X.509 certificates or pre-shared keys for authentication — one product deploying three
different primitives for three different properties. Traffic was captured on the tunnel interface
against the underlying interface to confirm that the cipher does what is claimed, which is the
verification step that makes the property a measurement rather than a belief. See [[wireshark]].

The lab also transferred the same file repeatedly under different cipher and authentication algorithm
choices and recorded the timings. **Security properties have a price, and the price is measurable** —
the same experimental instinct as [[cryptanalysis-by-measurement]], turned from attack to
engineering. TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes were inspected for the same reason.

## Why it belongs in a wiki about how things get built

The triad is a checklist for reading any design. For each of the three, ask what provides it, what
would falsify it, and whether that has been checked. Applied to this source set it immediately
separates the systems that *state* a security property from the ones that *demonstrate* it — the
distinction [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]] tracks throughout.
